title: Sound
seo_title: Year 7 Science: Sound Worksheets (Frequency, Amplitude, Echoes, Hearing)
standard_text: Frequencies of sound waves, measured in hertz (Hz); echoes, reflection and absorption of sound; sound needs a medium to travel, the speed of sound in air, in water, in solids; sound produced by vibrations of objects, in loudspeakers, detected by their effects on microphone diaphragm and the ear drum; sound waves are longitudinal; auditory range of humans and animals; pressure waves transferring energy.
meta_desc: Free Year 7 science worksheets on sound: vibrations, frequency and pitch, amplitude and loudness, the speed of sound, echoes, the ear and hearing ranges of animals. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Sound is vibrations travelling through a medium.
key_sub: Amplitude sets loudness; frequency sets pitch. No sound in a vacuum.
body_html:
How to think about it

Sound is a vibration that travels through a medium as a pressure wave.

  • Bigger amplitude: louder. Higher frequency (Hz): higher pitch. Humans hear about 20–20,000 Hz.
  • Sound travels fastest in solids and cannot travel through a vacuum. In air it is about 340 m/s.
  • Echoes are reflected sound. For an echo, the sound goes there and back, so halve the distance.
Example

Echo after 2 s at 340 m/s. Wall distance?

340 × 2 = 680 m there and back

Answer: 340 m

Example

Which is louder: amplitude 6 mm or 3 mm?

Bigger amplitude

Answer: 6 mm

Common mistakes

  • Thinking sound travels fastest in air.
  • Thinking sound can travel through space.
  • Thinking a louder sound has a higher frequency.

faq.a: A vibrating object makes the particles next to it vibrate, and the vibrations pass from particle to particle as a pressure wave. Sound cannot travel through a vacuum.

faq.q: What is the difference between pitch and loudness?
faq.a: Pitch depends on frequency (how many vibrations per second). Loudness depends on amplitude (how big the vibrations are).

faq.q: How do you work out distance from an echo?
faq.a: Multiply the speed of sound by the time to get the distance there and back, then halve it.

items.q: A pupil claps near a wall and hears the echo 2 s later. Sound travels at 330 m/s. How far away is the wall?
items.e: The sound goes there and back: 330 × 2 = 660 m, so the wall is 330 m away.

items.q: Sound travels at 340 m/s in air. How far does sound travel in 2 s?
items.e: Distance = speed × time = 340 × 2 = 680 m.

items.q: Sound travels at 330 m/s in air. How far does sound travel in 0.8 s?
items.e: Distance = speed × time = 330 × 0.8 = 264 m.
